topic: Day 2 · Secondary Prevention I — Antithrombotics & Carotid Revascularisation
speakerAffiliation: Virtual Teaching Hospital · Stroke Prevention Clinic
speakerBio: Times anticoagulation by infarct size and refers symptomatic carotids within the fortnight.
lectureHTML:
🎯 The case on the table

Your patient survived the stroke. Now comes the quieter, longer battle: making sure it never happens again. The right antithrombotic — and the right timing — can halve recurrence; the wrong one causes a fatal bleed or leaves an untreated clot source. This is where the mechanism you found in Session 12 becomes a prescription.

1 · Non-cardioembolic stroke — antiplatelets

  • Long-term: a single antiplatelet — clopidogrel (or aspirin ± dipyridamole).
  • Short-term DAPT: after a high-risk TIA or minor stroke, aspirin + clopidogrel for 21 days (CHANCE/POINT), or ticagrelor + aspirin in selected patients (THALES), then a single agent.
  • Do not continue long-term dual antiplatelet therapy — MATCH/SPS3 showed it adds bleeding without benefit.

2 · Cardioembolic (AF) — anticoagulation, and the timing question

For AF-related stroke, a DOAC is preferred over warfarin — the harder question is when to start it after an acute infarct.
💡 The "1–3–6–12 day" rule

Start anticoagulation later after larger strokes (higher haemorrhagic-transformation risk): roughly day 1 for a TIA, 3 for a small stroke, 6 for a moderate stroke, and 12 for a large stroke. The ELAN trial supports earlier initiation being reasonably safe in many patients, but the size-of-infarct principle still guides the individual decision.

3 · Carotid revascularisation — symptomatic stenosis

PointDetail
Who benefitsSymptomatic carotid stenosis 50–99% on the side of a non-disabling stroke/TIA (NASCET/ECST) — greatest benefit for 70–99%
WhenWithin 2 weeks of the event — benefit falls sharply with delay
HowCarotid endarterectomy is first-line; stenting (CREST) an option, higher periprocedural stroke risk in the elderly
AsymptomaticMuch smaller benefit — individualised, often medical therapy

4 · Intracranial stenosis

For symptomatic intracranial atherosclerosis, aggressive medical therapy beats stenting (SAMMPRIS: dual antiplatelet for 90 days plus intensive risk-factor control outperformed stenting, which had high periprocedural complications).

☠️ M&M — the AF stroke that was never anticoagulated

A patient with an AF-related stroke was discharged on aspirin because "the bleeding risk seemed high," and anticoagulation was deferred and then forgotten. He returned with a second, fatal cardioembolic stroke. Lesson: in AF, the recurrent-stroke risk usually far outweighs the bleeding risk, and aspirin is not an adequate substitute for anticoagulation. Set a clear start date using the infarct-size rule and make sure it actually happens.

5 · Take-home

  • Non-cardioembolic: single antiplatelet long-term; 21-day DAPT after high-risk TIA/minor stroke, then mono.
  • AF: DOAC, timed by infarct size (1–3–6–12 day rule; ELAN supports earlier).
  • Symptomatic carotid 50–99%: endarterectomy within 2 weeks.
  • Intracranial stenosis: medical therapy > stenting (SAMMPRIS).

moderatorQs.q: Single or dual antiplatelet after a non-cardioembolic stroke?
moderatorQs.answerHTML: Single agent long-term (usually clopidogrel), but a short 21-day course of dual antiplatelet (aspirin + clopidogrel) after a high-risk TIA or minor stroke reduces early recurrence (CHANCE/POINT), then step down to mono. Long-term DAPT is the trap — MATCH/SPS3 showed it only adds bleeding without further benefit.

moderatorQs.q: When do you start anticoagulation after an AF-related stroke?
moderatorQs.answerHTML: Timed to the infarct size and haemorrhagic-transformation risk — the pragmatic 1–3–6–12 day rule: roughly day 1 for a TIA, 3 for a small, 6 for a moderate and 12 for a large stroke. A DOAC is preferred over warfarin. The ELAN trial suggests earlier initiation is reasonably safe for many, but the size-of-infarct principle still guides the individual.

moderatorQs.q: Which carotids need revascularising, and how quickly?
moderatorQs.answerHTML: Symptomatic stenosis of 50–99% on the side of a non-disabling stroke/TIA, with the greatest benefit at 70–99% (NASCET/ECST) — and it must be done within about 2 weeks, because the benefit falls sharply with delay. Carotid endarterectomy is first-line; stenting is an alternative with higher periprocedural risk in older patients (CREST). Asymptomatic stenosis benefits far less.

audienceQs.q: Why not just use aspirin for an AF stroke — it's simpler?
audienceQs.answerHTML: Because aspirin is markedly inferior to anticoagulation for preventing cardioembolic stroke, while carrying its own bleeding risk. In AF the recurrent-stroke risk usually far outweighs the bleeding risk, so a DOAC (or warfarin where indicated) is the standard — substituting aspirin leaves the patient substantially under-protected.

audienceQs.q: Should we stent symptomatic intracranial stenosis?
audienceQs.answerHTML: Generally no. SAMMPRIS showed that aggressive medical therapy — 90 days of dual antiplatelet plus intensive risk-factor control — outperformed intracranial stenting, which had a high periprocedural complication rate. So intracranial atherosclerosis is treated medically, reserving intervention for selected refractory cases.
